name: W3C Web Annotation selectors and fuzzy re-anchoring. Canonical: Web Annotation Data Model (W3C Recommendation, 23 February 2017) plus the companion Web Annotation Vocabulary and Protocol; the selector classes are FragmentSelector, CssSelector, XPathSelector, TextQuoteSelector, TextPositionSelector, DataPositionSelector, SvgSelector, RangeSelector, and the refinement/state machinery (refinedBy, TimeState, HttpRequestState). Predecessor: Open Annotation Collaboration / Annotea. Reference implementations: the Hypothesis client (dom-anchor-text-quote, dom-anchor-text-position, dom-anchor-range, xpath-range), apache-annotator, anchorpoint, Semiont. The 'two XPaths' phrasing in the project's framing refers to RangeSelector, which stores a start and an end selector -- in the Hypothesis implementation a pair of XPaths plus string offsets inside the addressed elements.
kind: Standard (W3C Recommendation) plus a body of implementation practice and one independent measurement study. Not a library, not a benchmark, though the Hypothesis anchoring-test-tools repository is a de-facto test harness.
maturity: Standards-track and finished: W3C Recommendation since 2017, stable, no successor in progress. The implementation practice around it (fuzzy fallback chains) is production but explicitly non-normative -- the Recommendation defines what a selector MEANS and says essentially nothing about what to do when it fails to resolve. That gap is where every real system improvises, and it is why there is no interoperable re-anchoring behaviour despite an interoperable serialisation.
license: The specification is under the W3C Document Licence and the Software and Document Notice; using the vocabulary and data model imposes no obligation and is fine here. Implementations: the Hypothesis client and its dom-anchor-* modules are BSD-2-Clause/MIT-family, apache-annotator is Apache-2.0, google diff-match-patch (the fuzzy engine Hypothesis uses) is Apache-2.0. All permit use in this project. The relevant adoption is the data model and the fallback discipline, both of which are ideas rather than code.
keeps_and_discards: A selector keeps a description of a REGION, not the content of the region -- except that TextQuoteSelector deliberately keeps a copy of the selected text plus a bounded window of surrounding text. That exception is the whole point: it is the only selector that carries enough content to survive the loss of the structure it was recorded against. What the model discards is everything about WHY a region was selected and everything about the document outside the selected region and its immediate context. Concretely, the Hypothesis instantiation stores, per annotation, three selectors simultaneously: a RangeSelector (start and end XPath plus offsets), a TextPositionSelector (start and end character offsets into the whole document's text), and a TextQuoteSelector (the exact selected string plus a 32-character prefix and a 32-character suffix). Everything else about the page is discarded. For this project the transferable observation is that the redundancy is the mechanism -- three cheap, independently-failing descriptions of the same region, tried in order, is what buys robustness, and no single one of them is robust.
structure_preserved: Order and containment are preserved only insofar as the addressing scheme encodes them. XPathSelector and RangeSelector preserve full structural position, including nesting depth and sibling index, and are therefore the most structurally faithful and the most fragile. TextPositionSelector preserves linear order in the text stream and discards nesting entirely, which is why it survives structural change that leaves text intact and fails on any text insertion earlier in the document. TextQuoteSelector preserves nothing structural at all; it addresses a string in a string. RangeSelector's refinedBy machinery is the model's answer to composing them -- a range whose endpoints are themselves described by other selectors -- and it is the standard's clearest structural idea. Shadow boundaries are NOT addressed by the specification. XPath has no shadow-piercing semantics, and the Recommendation predates widespread shadow DOM; an annotation over content inside a shadow root has no standard address, which is a real gap for this project and means the standard supplies no precedent for the composed-tree addressing the sensor uses.
interactive_elements: Not handled. The model addresses regions of a document for the purpose of commenting on them; controls are addressable as elements but no state, affordance or interactivity is represented. There is no vocabulary for 'this annotation targets the checked state of this checkbox'. The nearest thing is the state machinery (HttpRequestState, TimeState), which describes how to retrieve a version of the resource rather than what the resource's controls were doing.
interactive_state_fidelity: Zero, and the omission is instructive rather than merely absent. The Web Annotation model's implicit document assumption is a static text resource whose only variability is over time (hence TimeState and Memento integration) rather than over interaction. A page whose content depends on which tab is open, which accordion is expanded, or which filter is applied has, under this model, no stable identity to anchor to at all -- the same URL yields different text depending on interaction state, and the model has no field for it. For a project addressing a LIVE composed DOM under mutation, this is the single largest respect in which the standard under-specifies the problem: it can tell you how to re-find a string, and it cannot tell you whether the document you are re-finding it in is in the same state. If the project adopts the selector discipline it should add an interaction-state field that the standard lacks, and should not pretend the standard covers it.
layout_awareness: None for the text and XPath selectors -- they are purely structural and lexical, which is a clean fit with no_layout_in_the_fold. SvgSelector is the exception and is explicitly geometric: it addresses a region by an SVG shape over the rendered resource, which is a layout-consuming selector and belongs, in this project's terms, strictly in the actuator layer. FragmentSelector with a media fragment can also carry spatial coordinates. The lesson is that the standard already draws the same line the project draws: geometric selectors are a separate class, used for images and media, not for text.
javascript_required: The data model requires nothing. Resolving a selector against a live page requires whatever it takes to produce the DOM being addressed -- which for a script-rendered page means the scripts have run, and for a static document means they have not. This is a hidden reproducibility hazard the standard does not name: an XPath recorded against a hydrated DOM will not resolve against the raw HTML of the same URL, and a TextPositionSelector's offsets differ between the two by however much text the scripts injected. Any stored selector is implicitly relative to a rendering mode, and the standard has no field for it.
evaluation_method: The standard itself has no evaluation; conformance is structural. The evaluation that matters is the independent study Quantifying Orphaned Annotations in Hypothes.is (Aturban, Alam, Nelson, Weigle; arXiv:1512.06195, TPDL 2015), whose method is the strongest in this whole item set and is directly imitable: take a large body of REAL annotations created by real users on real pages, attempt to re-anchor each against the live page today, and for those that fail, attempt to re-anchor against archived copies of the page retrieved through public web archives. The archive attempt is the crucial part -- it distinguishes 'the anchoring algorithm failed' from 'the text is genuinely gone', which is the distinction every naive re-anchoring evaluation collapses. Hypothesis also maintains anchoring-test-tools, which runs the client against real public-group annotations and reports anchored/orphaned counts; that is a regression harness rather than a study, and it is vendor-run.
corpus_size_and_origins: The orphan study covers 20,953 highlighted-text annotations drawn from Hypothesis's public corpus, collected in 2015. The number of DISTINCT ORIGINS is not stated in the abstract and matters a great deal, because Hypothesis's 2015 public usage was heavily concentrated in scholarly publishing, news commentary and a handful of heavily-annotated documents -- so the effective origin diversity is very likely far below 20,953 and the corpus is not a random sample of the web. It is also English-dominant and pre-dates both the current SPA era and widespread shadow DOM. Age is the other reach limit: the pages were annotated between roughly 2011 and 2015 and re-checked in 2015, so the measured survival window is short by the standards of an archive. Treat the figures as a lower bound on fragility for modern, script-heavy pages, not as a transferable rate. This is the same category of caveat as CleanEval's 58 English pages from 2007: a real measurement with a narrow reach.
reported_precision_recall: Two figure sets circulate and they disagree; both should be recorded rather than one chosen. The arXiv abstract for 1512.06195 reports that about 22% of highlighted-text annotations can no longer be attached to their live web pages, that only about 12% of those orphans could be recovered from public web archives (leaving roughly 88% of orphans permanently unrecoverable), and that 53% of the annotations that DO still attach are in danger of becoming orphans if the live page changes. A widely quoted variant of the same study reports 27% orphaned and 61% at risk. The discrepancy is most plausibly a version difference between the arXiv preprint and the published TPDL/Springer chapter, or a difference in the subset counted, and it has NOT been resolved here -- so the honest statement is that the measured orphan rate for real annotations over a roughly four-year window is 22-27% with 53-61% of survivors classified as fragile. Denominator in both cases is highlighted-text annotations attempted, not all annotations, and 'in danger' is the authors' classification of annotations whose anchoring depended on a selector they judged fragile rather than an observed failure. No precision/recall pair is published for the fuzzy matcher itself -- there is no reported figure for how often fuzzy re-anchoring lands on the WRONG text, which is the number this project most needs and which nobody has measured.
independent_oracle: Yes, and it is the best example in this item set. The orphan study's oracle is the web archive: an independent record of what the page said at annotation time, produced by a different system with different assumptions from the anchoring algorithm. It answers the question the anchoring algorithm cannot answer about itself -- whether a failure to anchor means the algorithm was too weak or the text was genuinely deleted. Its limitation is coverage: only ~12% of orphans had a usable archived copy, so the oracle is available for a small minority of the hard cases. The study's own recommendation follows directly and is the right one for this project too: archive the target at annotation time, i.e. store the bytes you anchored against, so the oracle is always available rather than 12% available. For a false-positive oracle -- catching fuzzy matches that anchor to the wrong place -- no published oracle exists; human adjudication of a sample is the only option and nobody has published one.
evidence_independence: The orphan study is genuinely independent: authored by the Old Dominion University web-science group, not by Hypothesis, using Hypothesis's public data. That independence is unusual and raises the study's weight considerably. The fuzzy-anchoring design description is a vendor blog post by Hypothesis and contains no numbers at all -- it states the strategy and the library used and, notably, discloses no thresholds, no acceptance tolerance and no measured success rate. The anchoring-test-tools statistics are vendor-run. So: the failure rate is independently measured, the success mechanism is vendor-described and unquantified. Any claim that fuzzy anchoring 'works well' traces to the vendor and to no measurement, and must not be laundered into the record as a result.
page_archetype_coverage: Not broken out by archetype in the published study, which is a significant gap given how much the failure mechanism should vary. Reasoning about it: a scholarly PDF or a versioned documentation page is near-static and should orphan rarely; a news article with a live comment section, a rotating related-articles rail, or an A/B-tested layout will shift both XPaths and global character offsets on every load, so TextPosition and Range selectors fail immediately and everything falls through to quote matching; a listing or feed page has no stable text at all and is effectively unanchorable. The single aggregate 22-27% therefore mixes near-0% and near-100% populations, and the same caution applies as to any single-number extraction score. [uncertain] -- this is inference from the mechanism, not a measured breakdown.
script_and_locale_behaviour: The model is Unicode-clean in principle: TextPositionSelector is defined over code points, and TextQuoteSelector over strings. In practice three problems bite. (1) Offsets are defined in code points, but JavaScript string operations are UTF-16 code units, so any implementation that uses raw JS indices mis-addresses text after an astral-plane character (emoji, rare CJK, historic scripts) -- a documented class of interoperability bug in this space. (2) Unicode normalisation is not specified: the same text in NFC and NFD is a different string to a quote selector, so a page re-served by a different pipeline can orphan every annotation on it with no visible change. (3) The 32-character prefix/suffix window used by Hypothesis is a fixed CHARACTER count, which in a whitespace-free script such as Chinese or Japanese carries far more semantic content than 32 characters of English, and in a script with heavy combining-mark use carries far less. So the discriminating power of the context window is script-dependent, which means the fuzzy matcher's false-positive rate is script-dependent, and nobody has measured it in any script other than English. A structure-agnostic claim should be script-invariant and this one demonstrably is not.
leaks_outward: The data model leaks nothing by itself. The deployed pattern does: a hosted annotation service receives the URL, the quoted text, and the surrounding 32 characters of every passage a user selects, which is a substantial content-and-behaviour disclosure to a third party. For this project the relevant reading is inverted -- the project stores its own anchors locally, so there is no outward leak, but the SHAPE of what an anchor stores (a quote plus context) is exactly the shape of a privacy-sensitive artifact, and if anchors are ever shared or exported they carry page content with them, including any personal data in the quoted region. An anchor is not a pointer; it is a small excerpt.
mechanism_detectability: Re-anchoring is a read-only DOM traversal plus string search. It performs no patching, opens no debugger, and installs no observer, so it is not directly detectable. Two indirect channels exist and are worth naming: a fuzzy search over the whole document text is CPU-visible and, on a large document, produces a timing signature a page could in principle observe through requestAnimationFrame jitter or long-task timing; and any implementation that highlights matches by wrapping text nodes in span elements MUTATES the DOM, which is trivially detectable by the page's own MutationObserver and can also break the page. That second point is the important one for this project: re-anchoring must be read-only. Hypothesis's client does inject highlight wrappers, which is fine for a user-facing annotator and unacceptable for a covert sensor.
countermeasures: Against detection: never mutate the document to record an anchor; hold anchors as offsets in an out-of-band structure. Against mis-anchoring: bound the fuzzy stage, which is the project's own stated instinct and is correct. Against silent drift: record, per anchor, WHICH strategy resolved it. Hypothesis's own strategy chain does not surface which of the four paths succeeded to the user, so a quote-matched anchor and an exact-XPath anchor are presented identically -- an anchor that fell through three fallbacks and matched fuzzily is a materially weaker claim than one that resolved on the first try, and collapsing them is the anti-pattern.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured anywhere. The specific unmeasured quantity is the cost of the fuzzy stage in false anchors: enabling fuzzy fallback converts some orphans into anchors, and an unknown fraction of those into WRONG anchors. The orphan study measures only the failure side (22-27% orphan) and cannot see the wrong-anchor side, because a wrong anchor looks like a success. The control that would answer it is straightforward and unpublished: take pages with known edit histories, apply known edits, re-anchor, and compare against the ground-truth post-edit region. Until someone does that, the fidelity cost of fuzzy matching is an unknown, and treating it as small is an assertion.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented. The model's state machinery (HttpRequestState, TimeState) captures request headers and a datetime for retrieval, which is the closest available hook -- HttpRequestState in particular can record the Accept and other headers needed to get the same representation back, and TimeState ties to a Memento datetime. Neither records whether the capture was behind a consent banner, paywall or login. This is a genuine hole: an annotation made on a logged-in view of a page and an annotation made on the public view address different documents at the same URL, and the model gives no way to say so. If the project extends the selector idea it should add a gate-state field; the standard supplies a natural place for it alongside the existing state classes.
determinism: The exact-match strategies are fully deterministic: an XPath either resolves or does not, and a text position either exists or does not. The fuzzy strategies are deterministic in the weak sense that the same input yields the same output for a fixed implementation and fixed thresholds -- Bitap over a fixed string with a fixed distance threshold is a pure function -- but they are NOT deterministic in the sense that matters, because the output depends on undisclosed threshold constants and on the whole document text, so an unrelated edit elsewhere in the page can change which candidate wins. Hypothesis's blog post discloses the algorithms (Bitap for matching, Myers diff for comparison, via a modified google diff-match-patch) and discloses no thresholds, which means the behaviour is not reproducible from the description alone. That is the precise reason the project's instinct to bound fuzzy matching is right.
determinism_across_versions: Drifts on three axes. (1) Implementation: a modified diff-match-patch means the behaviour is pinned to a fork, and changing the fork or its match_threshold/match_distance constants changes which anchors resolve, silently. (2) Browser: XPath resolution and the document's text content both depend on the parsed DOM, so parser changes (whitespace nodes, implied tbody, template/slot handling) shift both XPaths and global character offsets across browser versions. (3) Specification: the model is stable, but the shadow-DOM gap means implementations invent their own piercing syntax and those inventions are not interoperable. Anchors must therefore be treated as valid only relative to a recorded (implementation version, browser build) pair, and cross-version comparison is a re-anchoring problem in its own right.
reproducibility: Low against the live web, high against frozen bytes, and the study proves it: 22-27% of anchors could not be re-obtained at all after a few years, and only 12% of those were rescuable from archives. The actionable conclusion the authors state and this project should adopt verbatim is to archive the target at the time the anchor is created. In project terms: an anchor recorded against a live page is not reproducible evidence unless the bytes it was recorded against are stored alongside it. Given that 75% of the project's own corpus fetches live resources on every read, every anchor in that corpus currently has this defect.
failure_modes: Ranked by how they actually occur. (1) Structural edit invalidates the XPath -- any sibling inserted above the target shifts indices; this is the common case and it is why RangeSelector alone is inadequate. (2) Text insertion earlier in the document invalidates every subsequent TextPositionSelector offset; a single added paragraph orphans the entire rest of the page's position anchors. (3) The quoted text is edited or deleted, which no algorithm can fix and which the archive oracle is needed to distinguish from (1) and (2). (4) The context window becomes non-unique -- a 32-character prefix/suffix is not enough to disambiguate in repetitive documents (tables, code listings, legal boilerplate, listing pages), so quote matching anchors to the wrong occurrence. This is the silent-corruption mode and it is unmeasured. (5) The document is dynamic and its text differs per load, so anchors resolve differently on different loads of the same URL with no edit having occurred at all. (6) Shadow DOM or iframe content, for which there is no standard address. (7) Unicode normalisation or UTF-16-vs-code-point offset mismatch, which orphans everything past the first astral character.
failure_visibility: Mixed, and the mixture is the problem. Total failure is loud and well handled -- Hypothesis surfaces orphans explicitly as a category in the UI, which is good practice and worth copying. Partial failure is silent: an anchor that resolved via the fourth fallback is displayed identically to one that resolved exactly, and a fuzzy match onto the wrong occurrence is indistinguishable from a correct one to both the user and the system. There is even a filed defect in Hypothesis's own tracker noting that annotations can fail to anchor without being reported as orphans, i.e. the loud path is not exhaustive. The remedy is to make the resolution PATH a first-class recorded field, which converts the silent case into a graded one.
scale_limits: Per-anchor resolution cost is what matters. Exact XPath resolution is O(depth). Position resolution is O(1) given a text index. Context-first fuzzy matching is a bounded-error search over the document text -- Bitap is O(n * m / w) in document length n and pattern length m, so it is LINEAR IN THE DOCUMENT, not in the change. Selector-only fuzzy matching is the same over the whole text. Therefore the fallback chain's cost profile is a cliff: the first two strategies are constant-ish and the last two are whole-document scans, and a page where most anchors fall through costs O(anchors * document length). On a large document with many anchors this is the dominant cost and it is quadratic-ish in practice. Any budgeted design must cap the number of anchors allowed to reach the fuzzy stage per capture.
delta_cost_model: The standard defines no delta model; anchoring is a from-scratch resolution per load. That is a genuine mismatch with this project and the mismatch should be stated rather than papered over. What a bounded, delta-friendly version would look like, and what falls outside its per-change cost: an exact-match-first resolution is O(depth) per anchor and can be driven incrementally from mutation records, so anchors under an unchanged subtree cost nothing -- provided there is a cheap test for 'this subtree is unchanged', which a per-node content hash supplies. OUTSIDE that bound: (1) any anchor that falls through to fuzzy matching, which is O(document text) and unbounded by the size of the change -- this is the exception that must be named, and it is why the fuzzy stage must be rate-limited and recorded rather than run freely; (2) ancestor-index shifts, where one insertion invalidates every following sibling's XPath, making a delta of one produce O(n) anchor invalidations; (3) global text-offset invalidation, where one text insertion invalidates every subsequent position selector -- the single worst delta amplification in this item, and a decisive argument against storing global character offsets at all in a live-mutation setting; (4) initial load, where every anchor resolves from scratch; (5) content arriving inside a shadow root or iframe, which mutation records may not cover and for which no address exists.
reanchoring_stability: This is the item's core contribution and the numbers are: 22-27% of real annotations orphaned over a roughly four-year window against the live web, 53-61% of survivors classified as fragile, and only ~12% of orphans recoverable from public archives (Aturban et al., 20,953 annotations, 2015, independent of the vendor). The mechanism ranking that follows is: raw single XPath is the weakest; a RangeSelector pair of XPaths plus offsets is stronger only against edits that do not touch ancestors, and is not meaningfully stronger against the common case of a sibling insertion; global text position survives structural change and dies on any earlier text change; a quote plus bounded context is the only one that survives both, and it is the one that can silently land in the wrong place. RECOMMENDED BOUNDED DETERMINISTIC DESIGN for this project, satisfying the stated requirement that fuzzy matching not contaminate reproducibility: store four things per address -- (a) the positional xpath, (b) a content hash of the node's own text, (c) a content hash over the node's ordered child hashes (a Merkle node hash, which makes 'subtree unchanged' an O(1) test), and (d) a short exact quote with a bounded context window sized in code points and Unicode-normalised to NFC. Resolve in strictly this order, and record which step succeeded as a mandatory field: STEP 0, xpath resolves AND node hash matches -> confidence exact, cost O(depth); STEP 1, xpath resolves and node hash differs but child-hash set overlaps -> confidence exact-address-changed-content, cost O(depth); STEP 2, xpath fails, but the node hash is found at exactly one other address in the same parent's subtree -> confidence relocated-exact, cost O(subtree), and this step is where an ancestor-index shift is absorbed cheaply and deterministically; STEP 3, hash not found, exact string match of the quote-plus-context occurs at exactly one place in the document -> confidence quote-exact, cost O(document) but still EXACT and therefore reproducible; STEP 4, no exact match -> DO NOT fuzzy-match by default; record a miss with the reason. Fuzzy matching (Bitap or equivalent) is available only as an explicitly requested, explicitly recorded fallback that writes a confidence score, the edit distance, the number of competing candidates within threshold, and the threshold constants used, so that any result derived through it is identifiable and excludable from a reproducible run. Reject the match outright when more than one candidate falls within threshold -- ambiguity should orphan, not guess, because a wrong anchor is worse than a missing one and is the failure the literature has never measured. This gives a five-step chain in which steps 0-3 are deterministic and exact, step 4 is a recorded, bounded, ambiguity-refusing fallback, and the confidence field makes the distinction queryable rather than invisible.
adversarial_exposure: A quote selector stores raw page text, so it faithfully preserves any injected content in the quoted region and its context window -- an anchor is a small verbatim excerpt and inherits every injection property of the text it quotes. Two specific hazards. First, a page can DEFEAT anchoring cheaply by randomising DOM structure or inserting zero-width characters into text on every load, orphaning anchors at will; this is a plausible anti-archiving measure and the standard has no defence. Second and more seriously, a page can ATTACK a fuzzy anchor: because fuzzy matching accepts approximate matches within an undisclosed threshold, an adversary who knows the quoted text can plant a near-duplicate elsewhere in the document and cause the anchor to relocate onto attacker-chosen content. The refusal-on-ambiguity rule above is the direct mitigation and is the strongest argument for it. Without geometry, none of the selectors can tell whether the anchored region is visible; a quote selector anchors happily into a display:none block, so the model is layout-blind in exactly the way this project is and confers no additional protection.
provenance_carrying: Strong at the region level and this is the model's real strength for this project. An Annotation names its target with a source IRI plus a selector, so every anchored region carries origin and address by construction; the state classes add a retrieval datetime and request conditions. What is missing relative to what this project needs: shadow depth (no vocabulary), gate state (no vocabulary), the rendering mode the anchor was recorded against (no vocabulary), and which resolution strategy produced the current anchoring (not part of the model, which describes the recorded anchor and not the act of resolving it). The last one is the important addition -- the model records a claim about where something is and has no way to record how confident the current resolution of that claim is. A confidence-and-method field is the single most valuable extension to make.
roundtrip_safety: Selector serialisation is JSON-LD and round-trips cleanly as data. The interesting round-trip is semantic rather than syntactic: resolve a selector to a region, then re-derive a selector from that region, and check that the two selectors are equal. That is an oracle-free anchoring-fidelity test, it is cheap, it is not part of anyone's published practice, and it would catch offset-unit bugs, normalisation mismatches and off-by-one context windows immediately. It should be a standing test in this project. Escaping policy: a quote selector holds arbitrary page text and must be treated as untrusted data on every downstream path -- when an anchor's quote is rendered into markdown for a model, it needs the same escaping any other page-derived string needs, and the fixed 32-character window means an injected string can be split mid-construct, which is its own hazard.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not a token-emitting system, but it defines a very cheap unit worth reusing. An anchor -- exact quote plus a bounded context window plus an address -- is a compact, self-describing, provenance-carrying citation, on the order of 30-80 tokens depending on window size and script. That makes it the natural currency for the project's budgeted expansion: a child list can be presented as anchors rather than as content, so a model can see what is available and where it is before paying for it. On ordering: the confidence field should be emitted WITH the content, not in a footnote, because a model that reads a fuzzily-recovered quote without knowing it was fuzzily recovered will treat it as exact -- and given that position bias becomes recency-dominant past roughly half the context, a caveat placed early and content placed late is a caveat that will be ignored. Attach the confidence to the excerpt inline.
representation_cost: Per anchor, roughly: an XPath string (tens of bytes to a few hundred on deep DOMs), two integers, and the quoted text plus 64 characters of context. Trivially small individually; the cost is in the count. The relevant tradeoff for this project is the context window size: a larger window reduces ambiguity and therefore false anchors, and costs linearly in storage and tokens. 32 characters each side is Hypothesis's undocumented choice, is demonstrably too small to be unique in repetitive documents, and is script-dependent in its discriminating power. A window sized to reach uniqueness within the document -- grow until the quote-plus-context occurs exactly once, and record the achieved window -- is a better rule, is deterministic, and makes the ambiguity-refusal test above trivial to implement.
what_could_be_adopted: Four things, in order of value. (1) THE LAYERED SELECTOR DISCIPLINE ITSELF: record several independently-failing descriptions of the same location and resolve them in a fixed order. This is the standard's durable idea and it is directly applicable to the project's one-xpath key -- the key can stay one xpath while the RECOVERY record carries hash and quote alongside it, so the primary key stays clean and the fallbacks live in payload. (2) MANDATORY RECORDED RESOLUTION METHOD AND CONFIDENCE. The literature's single clearest defect is that a fuzzy match and an exact match are reported identically; making the path a field converts a silent degradation into a queryable one and satisfies the project's no-silent-degradation stance. (3) THE ARCHIVE-THE-TARGET-AT-ANCHOR-TIME RECOMMENDATION, which the orphan study makes explicitly and which the project's own 75%-live-fetch corpus currently violates. Storing the bytes is what makes an anchor's later failure diagnosable rather than merely observed. (4) REFUSE ON AMBIGUITY as a hard rule -- more than one candidate within threshold means orphan, not best guess. Explicitly NOT worth adopting: global document character offsets, which have the worst delta-amplification behaviour of any mechanism in this item and fail on any earlier text insertion; and unbounded fuzzy matching as a default path, for the reproducibility reason the project already identified and which the absence of any measured false-anchor rate makes impossible to justify.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Selectors describe positions and strings; none of them names a region nav or article, none embeds a learned or hand-tuned notion of what a region means, and the quote selector is pure content matching. No violation. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the text and XPath selectors; SvgSelector and spatial FragmentSelector are ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY, since they consume geometry by definition -- the standard already segregates them, so following the standard follows the constraint. o_delta: ADOPTABLE IN A BOUNDED FORM ONLY, with the exceptions named explicitly. Exact-match resolution driven from mutation records is O(depth) per affected anchor and respects the bound; the fuzzy fallback is O(document) and does not; global text offsets suffer O(n) invalidation from a single insertion and should be rejected outright on delta grounds; ancestor-index shifts amplify one mutation into a subtree of invalidations, which is a real exception to any O(delta) claim and is unavoidable with positional keys. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS; resolution runs against the real DOM by definition and there is no stub temptation. The one caution is that any evaluation must run against real captured pages with real edit histories, not synthetic mutations, or it measures nothing. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO CONFLICT, and a GAP -- the standard has no shadow-piercing address at all, so it neither requires nor tempts attachShadow patching; it simply cannot address content the sensor legitimately cannot reach, which is the correct behaviour. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is at the level of the data model and the layered discipline; the Hypothesis fuzzy fallback chain specifically is NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY in its unbounded form -- it demonstrates what the failure rates are and demonstrates, by publishing no thresholds and no false-anchor rate, exactly why an unbounded fuzzy stage cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline.
governance_signal_handling: The standard is silent on robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF and HTTP 402; annotation was framed as a user-agent activity on pages the user is already viewing, so crawler governance never arose. The one adjacent mechanism is HttpRequestState, which records the request conditions used to retrieve the representation and could carry an access-control or payment context if extended. Practically: an anchor stores an excerpt of a page, and if the page's governance signals forbid AI training or automated retention, storing the excerpt is the regulated act regardless of how small it is. Governance state belongs on the source resource record, resolved by URL prefix, not on the selector.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: An anchor is a stored excerpt of a third-party page plus its location, which means it is stored page content and therefore squarely inside whatever regime governs persistent retention -- the small size does not exempt it. Quoted text and its context window can contain personal data (names in an author byline, a comment thread, a profile page), and a context window is captured mechanically with no content filtering, so PII retention is unavoidable if anchors are taken over arbitrary pages. Two mitigations follow from the mechanism: store the hash-based recovery fields (node hash, child-hash) and treat the QUOTE as the optional, higher-risk layer that can be omitted or truncated for sensitive origins, since hashes are non-reversible and carry no content; and make anchors deletable by URL prefix so an erasure request removes the excerpts along with the nodes. The orphan study's advice to archive the target at anchor time pulls in the opposite direction from data minimisation and the tension should be acknowledged rather than resolved silently -- reproducibility wants more retention, the regulation wants less. [uncertain] on the specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject; the assessment here is structural.
